topics.title: PImpl Idiom (Pointer to Implementation)
topics.description: Hiding private implementation details and third-party headers behind an opaque pointer to speed up compilation.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The PImpl Idiom (Pointer to Implementation / Compilation Firewall) moves private data and methods into an internal struct defined only in the .cpp file.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Changing a private member in a header file forces every file that includes that header to recompile. PImpl eliminates compilation cascades and provides ABI stability.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Header declares struct Impl; std::unique_ptr<Impl> pImpl;. Definition lives in .cpp.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Client only includes the lightweight header; the heavy implementation and dependencies are isolated in the .cpp translation unit.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Compilation Firewall
callout.text: Header.hpp: struct Impl; unique_ptr<Impl> pImpl; (Zero 3rd-party includes!)\nHeader.cpp: struct Impl { HeavyWindowsSdk sdk; }; (Only this .cpp recompiles!)

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Widget delegates private operations to opaque struct Impl via std::unique_ptr.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Qt Framework (Q_D pointer), Windows API SDKs, Proprietary Closed-Source C++ SDK distributions.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use in public library headers to preserve ABI compatibility and minimize client compilation times.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use for small, performance-critical math structs where heap allocation overhead is unacceptable.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Fast build times; true encapsulation of private dependencies; stable binary ABI.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Extra heap allocation for Impl and pointer indirection overhead per call.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: PImpl with std::unique_ptr, Fast PImpl (placement new in fixed stack buffer).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Defining ~Widget() in the header file (causes compile error: cannot delete incomplete type Impl).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why must the destructor of a PImpl class be defined in the .cpp file?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Because std::unique_ptr<Impl> requires sizeof(Impl) to generate its default deleter. In the header, Impl is an incomplete type; defining the destructor in the .cpp file ensures Impl is fully defined.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Wrap a heavy DatabaseClient using the PImpl idiom.

practice.title: DatabaseClient PImpl
practice.problemStatement: Wrap a heavy DatabaseClient using the PImpl idiom.

referenceCode.code: class DbClient { struct Impl; std::unique_ptr<Impl> pImpl; public: DbClient(); ~DbClient(); };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering PImpl Idiom (Pointer to Implementation) is essential for advanced C++ systems design.

topics.title: CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern)
topics.description: Achieving compile-time static polymorphism without VTable and VPTR runtime overhead.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: CRTP is a C++ idiom where a class derives from a template base class instantiated with the derived class itself (class Derived : public Base<Derived>).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Allows static polymorphism with method overriding that is 100% inlined at compile time with zero VTable overhead.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Base class casts this to Derived* (static_cast<Derived*>(this)) and calls derived methods statically.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Zero indirect function pointer lookups; maximum performance in tight loops.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: CRTP Static Dispatch
callout.text: template <typename Derived> class Base { public: void speak() { static_cast<Derived*>(this)->speakImpl(); } };

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: BaseProcessor dispatches statically to FastAudioProcessor without virtual functions.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: High-Frequency Trading (HFT) matching engines, Eigen matrix math library, PyBind11 bindings.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use in performance-critical code where virtual dispatch overhead or cache misses are bottlenecks.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if you need runtime heterogeneous collections (e.g. vector of mixed objects).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Zero runtime overhead; allows complete compiler inlining.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Complex template compiler error messages.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: CRTP Mixins, CRTP Static Interfaces, CRTP Object Counters.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to mark derived methods public or friend with the base class.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does CRTP differ from standard runtime polymorphism?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: CRTP resolves method binding at compile time via template instantiation (zero runtime cost, inlinable), whereas runtime polymorphism resolves methods at runtime via a VTable lookup (indirect branch).

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement a generic CRTP Cloneable mixin that automatically provides clone().

practice.title: CRTP Cloneable Mixin
practice.problemStatement: Implement a generic CRTP Cloneable mixin that automatically provides clone().

referenceCode.code: template<class D> struct Cloneable { std::unique_ptr<D> clone() const { return std::make_unique<D>(*static_cast<const D*>(this)); } };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern) is essential for advanced C++ systems design.

topics.title: Type Erasure (std::function & Custom Erasures)
topics.description: Encapsulating objects of any type that support a given interface without requiring a common inheritance hierarchy.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Type Erasure is a technique that provides a unified, polymorphic interface to unrelated concrete types without forcing them to inherit from a common base class.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Allows storing function pointers, lambdas with captures, and custom function objects uniformly in std::function.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Combines templates (compile time) with inheritance and virtual functions (runtime) hidden inside an internal bridge wrapper.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: std::function<void()> can hold any callable: free function, lambda, or member function bind.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Type Erasure Anatomy
callout.text: std::function / std::any / custom erasures store a template Concept<T> inside an opaque non-template interface!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: EventDispatcher stores free functions and stateful lambdas uniformly via type-erased std::function.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: std::function, std::any, std::move_only_function (C++23), Adobe Type Erasure library.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when you want duck-typing flexibility in C++ without rigid inheritance coupling.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use when template generics or standard interfaces suffice with less boilerplate.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Duck-typing in strongly typed C++; callers don't need to inherit from base classes.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Minor dynamic memory allocation and indirect call overhead in std::function.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: std::function, std::any, Custom Value-Semantic Type Erasure.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Excessive dynamic allocations when passing small lambdas (mitigated by Small Buffer Optimization - SBO).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does std::function implement Type Erasure internally?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: It holds a pointer to an internal abstract CallableBase and template derived CallableImpl<Functor> that stores and invokes the actual callable.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Build a type-erased container that prints any object with operator<<.

practice.title: Type-Erased Printable Container
practice.problemStatement: Build a type-erased container that prints any object with operator<<.

referenceCode.code: class AnyPrintable { struct Concept { virtual void print() = 0; }; /* template Model<T> */ };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Type Erasure (std::function & Custom Erasures) is essential for advanced C++ systems design.

topics.title: Function Objects, Lambdas & Callback Architecture
topics.description: Modern event-driven design using lambdas, closures, std::bind, and asynchronous callbacks.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Function Objects (Functors) and Lambdas are objects that can be called like functions using operator().

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Enables clean callback-driven architectures (e.g. Button click handlers, asynchronous network response callbacks) without rigid inheritance.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Lambdas generate anonymous compiler structs with captured variables stored as member fields.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Pass std::function<void(const Response&)> as callback handlers.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Lambda Capture Semantics
callout.text: [=] captures by value (copy); [&] captures by reference (watch out for dangling stack references!); [this] captures member pointer.

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: AsyncHttpClient executes modern lambda callback with captured local session context.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Asynchronous I/O (Boost.Asio, libuv), GUI button listeners, threading task delegations.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use for event callbacks, custom container sorting comparators, and filter predicates.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not capture local references [&] in asynchronous callbacks that outlive the stack frame (dangling reference bug).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Concise, expressive, inline callback definitions.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Capturing large state by value incurs copy overhead.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Stateless Lambdas, Stateful Closures, Generic Lambdas (C++14), Template Lambdas (C++20).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Capturing local variables by reference in asynchronous background tasks.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is a dangling reference bug in C++ lambda captures?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: If a lambda captures a local stack variable by reference ([&x]) and the lambda executes asynchronously after the enclosing function has returned, accessing x causes undefined behavior / crash.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Build a Timer utility accepting std::function callback executed on tick.

practice.title: Timer Callback Handler
practice.problemStatement: Build a Timer utility accepting std::function callback executed on tick.

referenceCode.code: class Timer { public: void onTick(std::function<void()> cb) { cb(); } };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Function Objects, Lambdas & Callback Architecture is essential for advanced C++ systems design.
